scenario.context: PennyPal is a budgeting app. Only 38% of new users finish onboarding. The flow has 7 screens: sign-up, permissions, bank linking, goal setting, categories, tutorial, dashboard. Analytics show the biggest drop is at bank linking (screen 3), and 55% of users deny the notification permission.

steps.task: Write 3 testable hypotheses in the form We believe… because… so we expect…, each with a metric.
hints: Tie each one to evidence in the scenario.

items.text: We believe asking users to link a bank on screen 3 causes drop-off because it asks for trust before showing value, so showing a sample dashboard first should lift completion from 38% to 46%.
items.metric: Metric: onboarding completion rate; guardrail: % with a linked account by day 7.

items.text: We believe 7 screens is too long because most users who leave do so by screen 4, so cutting to 4 screens should add 5 points of completion.
items.metric: Metric: completion rate and time to finish.

items.text: We believe users deny notifications because they do not see the benefit, so adding a one-line benefit before the prompt should raise the grant rate from 45% to 60%.

reference.whyItWorks: Each hypothesis has one change, a reason, a number, and a metric you can measure.
commonMistakes: Bundling several changes in one hypothesis
rubric: Uses the We believe… because… so we expect… form

scenario.context: SketchPad is a design tool with a 14-day free trial and 6% trial-to-paid conversion. Data: 60% of trial users never create a second project; paying users mostly use templates and invite teammates; most teams say they need more than 14 days to decide.

steps.task: Write 4 hypotheses, rank them by how risky the underlying assumption is, and design a test for the top one.
hints: A good test names the variant, the metric and the run length.

items.text: H1 (top): We believe trial users stall because a blank canvas gives no starting point, so a template-first start should raise the second-project rate from 40% to 55% and conversion from 6% to 7.5%.
items.metric: Metric: second-project rate within 7 days; secondary conversion at day 14.

items.text: H2: We believe invites drive conversion because teams pay, so prompting an invite on day 2 should raise conversion among invited users.
H3: We believe 14 days is too short for team decisions, so extending team trials to 21 days should lift team conversion.
H4: We believe pricing is seen too late, so showing the pricing page on day 3 should reduce last-day drop-off.

content.notes: Ranking: H1 first, then H2, H3, H4. Test for H1: 50/50 A/B test on new trials; primary metric second-project rate within 7 days; secondary conversion at day 14; guardrail: time to first project; run for at least 2 full weekly cycles and until each arm has a few hundred users.

reference.whyItWorks: Hypotheses link to specific data, and the test has a variant, metric, guardrail and duration.
commonMistakes: Testing the easiest idea instead of the riskiest
Tests that end after a few days

scenario.context: HomeFix is a home-services marketplace. 28% of customers rebook within 90 days. The top 20% of providers get 70% of repeat bookings. Customers say they struggle to find the same provider again. Providers admit they sometimes take regular customers off the platform to avoid the fee.

steps.task: Write 4 hypotheses covering demand, supply, trust and timing. For each give the riskiest assumption, the cheapest test, and a result that would prove it wrong.
hints: Cover both sides of the marketplace.
State the falsifying result before running the test.

items.text: H1 (demand): We believe rebooking is hard because re-finding a provider is cumbersome, so a Book again button should lift 90-day rebooking by 4 points. Riskiest assumption: customers want the same provider. Test: button for 50% of customers. Falsified if button use is under 5% or rebooking does not move.
H2 (supply): We believe ranking providers with strong repeat rates higher will lift conversion. Test: two pilot zones. Falsified if conversion falls or new providers starve and fill rate drops.

H3 (trust and leakage): We believe providers move customers off-platform because of the fee, so a lower fee on repeat jobs with the same customer (for example 15% to 8%) should raise on-platform repeats. Falsified if repeats do not rise or margin loss exceeds gain.

H4 (timing): We believe service needs recur on cycles (for example AC service every 6 months), so reminders at 5 months should create bookings. Falsified if open rate is under 10% or no bookings follow.
items.metric: Metric: reminder open rate; bookings from reminders.

reference.whyItWorks: Covers all drivers of repeat behaviour and sets stop conditions in advance.
rubric: Demand, supply, trust and timing covered
